The Fork-tailed threadfin bream Nemipterus furcosus is a commercially important nemipterid that inhabits the continental shelf waters of the Indo-West Pacific region. Field surveys based on trawl catches have provided comprehensive life-history data for this species, which displays a moderately rapid growth trajectory. The maximum standard length attained by individuals in wild populations has been documented as 24 centimeters [Li = 24 centimeters], representing the ultimate size ceiling for this species. This asymptotic length is generally consistent with values reported for other medium-bodied members of the genus Nemipterus occupying similar tropical demersal habitats. The onset of reproductive capability occurs considerably earlier in the growth trajectory, with size at puberty recorded at 15.8 centimeters [Lp = 15.8 centimeters] standard length, indicating that individuals begin investing in gonadal development well before reaching their maximum somatic dimensions. Such an early onset of maturation relative to asymptotic size is a common pattern among tropical demersal teleosts that experience relatively high adult mortality rates. This life-history strategy allows individuals to achieve some reproductive output before the increased risks associated with larger body size and greater foraging exposure accumulate over time.


The mass at birth for Nemipterus furcosus is remarkably low, reflecting the pelagic egg stage characteristic of most nemipterid fishes. Based on an egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters, the calculated wet weight of a newly fertilised ovum is 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], a value that underscores the extremely small starting point from which this species must accumulate tissue throughout its life cycle. The egg is a transparent, spherical, pelagic type that undergoes rapid embryonic development following external fertilisation during broadcast spawning events. Once the yolk-sac larva emerges through chorion rupture, the endotrophic larval phase is brief, lasting only until mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding. This minuscule initial mass imposes a period of high vulnerability during the early larval stages, when starvation and predation pressure are most intense. Survivorship through this critical window depends heavily on the temporal match between hatching events and the seasonal availability of suitable planktonic prey organisms, a factor that can drive substantial interannual variation in recruitment strength for this species.


Under the sustained thermal conditions of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] that prevail in its tropical reef-adjacent habitats, Nemipterus furcosus exhibits a lifespan estimated at 3,650 days [am = 3,650 days], which corresponds to a maximum longevity of approximately ten years. This lifespan was derived from length-frequency analysis and validated through otolith readings conducted on specimens collected across the species geographic range. Such a decadal lifespan is relatively typical among demersal nemipterids, although it places this species at the more moderately-lived end of the continuum when compared to some deeper-water congeners that may exceed fifteen years of age in cooler thermal regimes. The longevity record highlights a life history that balances modest annual reproductive output against a multi-year reproductive window, allowing iteroparous adults to contribute to population replenishment across numerous spawning seasons. The consistency of the 28 °C [T = 28 °C] thermal environment in these tropical waters likely plays a key role in maintaining the metabolic and developmental rates that underpin this decadal lifespan.


As individuals approach their asymptotic size, the maximum wet weight recorded for Nemipterus furcosus reaches approximately 230 grams [Wwi = approximately 230 grams], a mass that is attained only by the oldest and largest specimens within a population. This ultimate body mass reflects the cumulative somatic growth achieved across the entire lifespan under the prevailing environmental conditions. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty, when the gonads first become active and vitellogenesis in females commences, is substantially lower at 40 grams [Wwp = 40 grams], representing only a fraction of the ultimate mass. This divergence between the mass at sexual maturation and the maximum adult mass indicates a growth pattern in which reproductive activity begins relatively early, but somatic expansion continues steadily thereafter for several additional years. The energetic demands of maintaining both continued somatic growth and concurrent reproductive investment are considerable, and trade-offs between these competing physiological demands likely shape the interannual patterns of fecundity and egg quality observed in this species. Such patterns are consistent with the life-history profiles of many tropical iteroparous teleosts that inhabit productive continental shelf ecosystems.


Reproductive output in Nemipterus furcosus has been quantified through histological examination of gravid ovaries collected during the peak spawning season. The number of hydrated oocytes per spawning female provides a direct estimate of batch fecundity, which represents the eggs released during a single spawning event within the extended reproductive period. Mature females produce approximately 40,000 to 70,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 40,000 to 70,000 eggs per spawning event], with multiple such events occurring throughout the protracted spawning season that spans several months in tropical waters. The capacity for multiple spawning events within a single reproductive season is a common strategy among demersal nemipterids, allowing females to spread reproductive risk across time. The spawning frequency has been estimated at approximately one event every three to four weeks during the height of the reproductive period [F_R_i = approximately one event every three to four weeks during the height of the reproductive period], a pattern that likely maximizes the probability that at least some cohorts of pelagic larvae encounter favorable feeding conditions during their critical early life stages.
